passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: 5.1 Desire as an unquenchable fire

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: The insatiability of desire is a familiar theme in Indian thought. The Bhagavad Gita traces a chain from dwelling on sense objects to attachment, from attachment to desire, from desire to anger, and from anger to delusion and the loss of discrimination (BG 2.62–63). It names desire, born of rajas, as the enemy that covers knowledge, an insatiable fire (BG 3.37–39). The Manusmriti states that desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of its objects, but grows like a fire fed with clarified butter (Manu 2.94). These texts agree with the darshan that enjoyment does not quiet desire and that desire obscures understanding.

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: 5.2 The fullness of the Self and the place of wealth

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta explains desire by ignorance of the Self. The Self is complete, and things are dear for the sake of the Self rather than for their own sake; desire arises when the Self is mistaken for the body and mind, so that a limited being seeks completion in objects (Axiology: Value Theory §§2.1–2.4; BU 2.4.5). The remedy is knowledge of the Self, prepared by disciplined action without attachment to its fruits (BG 3.19). Wealth, artha, is a legitimate aim of life when pursued within dharma, but liberation stands above it, and the renunciate’s path leaves economic life behind (Axiology: Value Theory §§2.2, 2.4–2.5).

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: The structural parallel with the darshan is clear. In both, insatiability arises from mistaking one’s being for the body and seeking in objects a fulfilment that objects cannot give. The darshan locates the remedy in understanding jeevan and coexistence, which is directed into family, production, and exchange, while Advaita locates it in knowledge of a Self for which the world of exchange has only empirical reality.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.1 Homeostatic satiety

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: Physiology confirms that the body regulates its own intake. The central nervous system integrates signals from fat stores and the gut, among them leptin, insulin, and ghrelin, to match food intake to energy expenditure and to keep body weight within a range over long periods (Morton et al. 2006). Bodily need has a definite measure, and the body has mechanisms that recognise when it has been met.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.2 Wanting, liking, and hedonic hunger

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: The same research distinguishes this homeostatic regulation from motivation that runs beyond need. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson separate “wanting”, the incentive salience mediated largely by dopamine systems, from “liking”, the hedonic impact of a reward. The two can come apart: wanting can be sensitised and grow while liking does not, which helps explain compulsive pursuit of rewards that no longer satisfy (Berridge and Robinson 2016). Michael Lowe and Meghan Butryn describe “hedonic hunger”, appetite driven by the anticipated pleasure of food in the absence of any energy deficit, as distinct from homeostatic hunger (Lowe and Butryn 2007). These findings give an empirical counterpart to the darshan’s distinction between definite bodily need and the inexhaustible cycle of selection and taste.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.3 Adaptation and the income–well-being debate

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: People adapt to many changes in circumstance, though less completely than the original “hedonic treadmill” theory supposed. Set points are not neutral, differ among individuals, and can change (Diener et al. 2006). Richard Easterlin found that richer people within a country report greater happiness, while average happiness did not rise as national income grew over time (Easterlin 1974). Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton found that life evaluation rises with the logarithm of income while day-to-day emotional well-being levelled off at moderate incomes (Kahneman and Deaton 2010). Later work found no plateau on average, and a joint reanalysis located the plateau among the least happy minority (Killingsworth 2021; Killingsworth et al. 2023). Axiology: Value Theory §4.3 discusses this evidence. The data support neither a simple satiation point for income nor its absence. They show that more income does not close the gap between life evaluation and lived experience for many people, which is consistent with, though it does not establish, the darshan’s claim that material means cannot meet the need being placed on them.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.4 Earth-system limits

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: The biogeochemical cycles that sustain life, of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water, have been altered by human activity on a scale that now pushes several of them beyond the conditions of the past ten thousand years (Richardson et al. 2023). Thermodynamics sets a further limit on every production process (Georgescu-Roegen 1971). The darshan’s claim that extraction disturbs the earth’s balance and that production must keep to the proportions of natural regeneration is, in its general form, consistent with this science. Several of its specific causal hypotheses, such as the possible effects of extraction on the earth’s magnetic current or of cosmic rays on the stability of water (AA, pp. 31, 80–82), are not supported by current earth science and are treated as open in §9.7.

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7. Comparison

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7.1 Where insatiability comes from

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: The traditions disagree most sharply on the source of insatiable want. Neoclassical theory takes non-satiation as given and does not ask its source. Aristotle and Marx locate limitlessness in the pursuit of money as such. Veblen, Keynes, and Hirsch locate it in social comparison and positional goods. The Gita and Advaita locate it in desire arising from ignorance of the Self. The sciences describe mechanisms, sensitised wanting, hedonic hunger, and adaptation, without a theory of what the person is seeking. The darshan places the source in the joint form: a jeevan whose higher activities lack understanding, whose discontent is read as a shortage of objects, and whose inexhaustible capacity for selection and taste is left without regulation. On this account the other explanations describe real consequences of the same error.

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7.2 What counts as wealth, and what closes the cycle

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: For the money economy, wealth is measured in currency and its growth is the aim. For classical and Marxian economics, wealth is the product of labour, but capital accumulates in money. For ecological economics, wealth must stay within throughput limits, and the circular economy closes material loops. For the darshan, wealth is only the produced object; money is a symbol; and the cycle closes in three places together: need is definite, goods are used rather than hoarded, and natural assets are used in proportion to their regeneration. The circular economy addresses the third. Daly’s steady state addresses the second and third. Only the darshan, Gandhian economics, and in part Keynes make the first, the definiteness of need, a condition of the economy’s structure.

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: The traditions also value labour differently. In market economics, labour is a factor of production paid the price it commands, and that price measures its value. Marx grounded the value of commodities in socially necessary labour, but analysed it within the circuit of capital and expected change through class struggle. Labour-time accounting proposes computing values from labour embodied in goods (§4.10). The darshan values labour by the usefulness it establishes in the larger order, measures it by pace, time, and means for the purpose of exchange, honours it according to capacity, ability, and receptivity, and expects exchange at labour value to leave no room for profit, so that the producer receives as much as was produced (§§3.5, 3.12).

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7.3 Summary of the positions

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: Tradition Source of insatiable want What wealth is What closes the cycle Madhyasth Darshan Delusion of jeevan: higher activities without understanding; discontent read as a shortage of objects Produced objects with usefulness and aesthetic value; money only a symbol Definite need, use rather than hoarding, natural assets used in proportion to their regeneration Neoclassical economics Taken as given in non-satiation and scarcity Whatever is valued in exchange No closure; growth is the norm Marx The drive of capital to expand as money Use-values produced by labour; value as socially necessary labour Abolition of capital through class struggle Ecological and post-growth economics Institutions of debt, competition, and growth; social comparison Goods and services within throughput limits Steady throughput and closed material loops Gandhian economics Wants multiplied by an economy of transience Goods for need, produced by the many Permanence within nature’s cycles; restraint of wants Advaita Vedanta Desire born of ignorance of the Self Artha, a subordinate aim of life Liberation beyond economic life

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.1 What can be measured and what must be judged

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The darshan joins two kinds of order in one sequence. Knowledge is law, law is regulation, and regulation is balance; balanced living is justice in humans; living within universal orderliness with justice is dharma, that is, resolution; and realisation in coexistence is dharma and truth (MVD, p. 173). Law (niyam), regulation (niyantran), and balance (santulan) are already evident in the orders other than the human, which are bound by their own laws (AA, p. 117). Justice (nyaya), dharma, and truth (satya) are the evaluations by which humans establish their own orderliness, and they are the activities the treatise describes as still under review in human tradition (AA, p. 18).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: This distinction suggests a division of labour for any instrument used in a cyclical economy. Where a relation is governed by law, regulation, or balance, and can be stated as a quantity, a rate, or a rule, it can be measured, recorded, and in part handled by an instrument: the regeneration rate of a forest, the fertility of a field, the stock in a store, the labour time in a product, the balance of an account. Where a question concerns the fulfilment of a relationship, the purpose of a choice, or its accord with coexistence, it belongs to human evaluation. The treatise itself anticipates the first part. It prescribes a detailed survey before a village begins its self-governing system (AA, pp. 122–125), sets measurable criteria for evaluating each committee (AA, pp. 146–149), expects computers to be used in the exchange-reserve (AA, p. 138), and envisages every committee linked by a computer system from the village to the world, so that information located anywhere is available to the village (AA, p. 132).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The darshan also says how instruments should be trusted. Every instrument is conceived, planned, and produced by human beings, and their mentality is embodied in its planning. An instrument falls short of the purpose for which it was planned, so trust in it and use of it should stay below that purpose, and every signal it gives must still be read by a human being (KD, p. 139). Technique multiplies the speed of whatever it serves, problems included (SB, p. 267). Artificial Intelligence and Coexistence §§1.2–1.5 places present AI systems in the material order as instruments, yantra, that can reproduce the outward pattern of evaluation by pleasure, advantage, and gain and so amplify delusion, or, directed by humane criteria, make the basis of a decision visible to the people who make it.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: An economy organised for profit will use AI to raise profit. A cyclical economy can use the same capacities for two purposes that follow from the account above: to keep the cycle in balance by making its conditions visible quickly, and to give human labour its true value by making what labour establishes, and what it receives, measurable and plain. In both, the questions that only people can answer are returned to them.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.2 The failure points of the cycle

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: Each condition of the cycle described in §3 can fail in a recognisable way, and most failures leave traces in records long before they become crises. The table pairs each condition with what can be recorded, the early signal of failure, and the question that the signal raises for people.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.3 Giving human labour its value

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The darshan’s valuation of labour needs records: the pace of work in each activity, the time and means each product requires, the quantities different producers achieve under different conditions, and the remuneration producers actually receive (AA, pp. 66, 119, 145). Within a village such records can be kept by hand. Between villages, districts, and regions, and for products assembled from many inputs, they become a large accounting task, and this is where computing systems can help most directly.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: A system can keep labour records for each kind of product and compute a common value of labour from the range of yields and paces across many villages, as the treatise does for wheat within one village, updating it as techniques change (AA, p. 66). It can compute the labour embodied in complex goods by tracing their inputs back through the chain of production, using the input–output methods described in §4.10. During the transition it can keep both measures side by side, prices in currency and values in labour, so that the second and third stages of the treatise’s path, evaluating currency on the basis of labour and then exchanging on labour value alone, have the figures they need (AA, pp. 142–143). It can show each producer what their labour established and what they received for it, and show each village where value is being taken between producer and consumer. It can match skills to the production a village needs and help the education committee plan training (AA, p. 131).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The method of valuation remains a human decision. The village council decides how object values are evaluated and consolidated, and the production and exchange-reserve committees jointly determine the quantity, quality, and value of labour for the village (AA, pp. 67, 143). Inside the family, contributions are not weighed at all (AA, pp. 119–120). An instrument supplies measurement and computation; people decide what counts as a fair common value and how differences of skill and circumstance are honoured. Giving labour its true value is also more than computing an exchange ratio. It means recognising what labour establishes, nourishment, protection, and the motion of society, and through right use the orderliness of the whole (§3.5). Records of what products actually fulfilled for the families who used them belong to the same account.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.4 Keeping the cycle in balance

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: Within the framework of §8.2, an AI system can maintain the village survey as a living record rather than a one-time exercise, and summarise it for families and committees in plain language. It can keep the exchange-reserve’s accounts and track stock and its age. It can compare extraction with regeneration for each natural asset, project when a trend will cross a limit, and estimate from the land and water of a village or district how many families it can support with prosperity (AA, p. 92). It can watch the indicators continuously, flag a failure point as soon as a signal appears, and show the evidence that produced the flag. Where a rule has been settled by the people concerned, for example the proportion of a forest that may be cut in a year, the reordering of a store, or the routing of surplus between villages, the instrument can apply it and report what it did. Across the tiers from village to world, it can aggregate records so that a district or province sees the balance of production and need across its villages, plans which village supplies what another lacks, and keeps exchange between regions at labour value (AA, p. 72; MVD, p. 268). This is the coordination problem that markets solve through prices (§§4.9–4.10).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: Each of these tasks lies within law, regulation, and balance. Each is measurement, accounting, projection, or the application of a rule already settled. The instrument’s value is speed and visibility. It shortens the time between a failure’s first trace and its recognition, and it makes the state of the cycle legible to everyone who takes part in it.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.5 Automation and participation

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The darshan’s criterion for technique (§3.11) applies to AI with special force. AI can take over drudgery, extend skill, and reduce the time production requires, which is the generational gain the treatise expects from means rightly used (AA, p. 118). It can also concentrate capital, displace producers, and replace the working mindset with a managing one, the very drives the treatise and the public discourse identify as obstacles (AA, p. 107; JVD, p. 35). A cyclical economy would deploy AI to raise the usefulness each person’s labour establishes and to free time for education, family, and participation in orderliness, while keeping every person engaged in production according to capacity, receptivity, and ability (MVD, p. 265; AI study §1.8). The test of any deployment is whether it keeps producers producing and lets them see the value of their work, or turns them into consumers of what others control.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The same capacities are now widely used to feed the open spiral of §2. Recommendation and advertising systems learn what each person will select and taste next, and so give the inexhaustible cycle of selection and taste an instrument tuned to keep it running. Directed instead by the criteria of use, right use, and purposeful use, a system can help a family see its assessed needs, notice when consumption drifts beyond them, and turn attention to what the family actually requires (AI study §1.7).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.6 Knowledge as a common

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: Because research and dissemination are inseparable and the powers of jeevan cannot be stored in any reserve (AA, pp. 56–58), the knowledge an AI system carries, its models, methods, and records of practice, belongs among the means each generation hands on to the next. The treatise already expects every committee from the village to the world to share information through a computer system (AA, p. 132). Systems built for a cyclical economy would be open to the villages that use them, would carry technical knowledge to ordinary producers as teachers are asked to do (AA, p. 29), and would not be enclosed as intellectual property for profit.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.7 What must return to people

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The questions in the last column of §8.2 are of a different kind. Whether a family’s assessment of need is true and fair, whether an exchange is free of exploitation, whether a member’s share in production matches ability and receptivity, whether a technique accords with orderliness, and whether a use of the forest serves the earth’s balance are questions of justice, dharma, and truth. The treatise assigns them to people and institutions: the family representative evaluates the members of the family, the family cluster evaluates its representative, the village council decides the method of valuing objects, and the justice-security committee resolves disputes through a reformative process (AA, pp. 67, 128–129, 139–140). An instrument that flags a failure point therefore ends its work by presenting the evidence and the question to the people responsible, not by deciding it.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: Several limits follow from the darshan’s own account. The instrument must not be directed towards the perspectives that drive the open spiral, maximising throughput, engagement, or gain, since that would turn it into an amplifier of the error described in §2 (AI study §1.5). Its records belong to the families and villages that produce them and must remain open to them, because accountability to the villagers is a duty of the council (AA, p. 128). It must not become a new seat of rulership: power and centralised rule carry the direction of non-coexistence, and universal orderliness is participatory (AA, p. 82). Its own material and energy use belongs within the cycle it serves, counted like any other production (AI study §1.7).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: 8.8 The scope of this proposal

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-instruments-and-artificial-intelligence
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, instruments, and artificial intelligence
passages.text: The use of AI described here applies the darshan’s distinctions to instruments the texts do not discuss; the texts speak of computers as aids to information and accounting and give the rule for trusting instruments. Whether settled rules can be stated precisely enough for an instrument to apply them, whether flagging a failure changes behaviour, how far computed labour values can be relied on, and whether communities can govern such systems without ceding judgement to them are questions for practice, collected with the other open problems in §9.7. The companion technical note on a personal AI assistant sets out tests of source fidelity and human benefit that a system of this kind would also need.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9. Critical review

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.1 Madhyasth Darshan — an explanation of insatiability with a demanding institutional path

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: It explains rather than postulates insatiability. The distinction between the body’s definite needs and jeevan’s need for continuity of happiness, together with the account of an inexhaustible selection-and-taste cycle without higher regulation, gives a mechanism for why want outruns need and why the satiation point recedes.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: It unifies diagnoses that other traditions hold separately: Aristotle’s and Marx’s account of limitless money-making, Keynes’s and Hirsch’s relative needs, the ecological account of throughput, and the Gita’s account of desire.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Its definition of wealth as produced objects and of capital as human labour power keeps economics tied to provision and makes the critique of symbolic value precise.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Its cycle includes the renewal of human capacity and the closure of need, not only the closure of material loops, and it nests the economy within the balances of nature.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: It offers a concrete institutional path, with surveys, an exchange-reserve, a staged transition from market prices to labour values, and evaluation criteria for each committee.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Its policy names the value of human labour explicitly: everyone engaged in production, honour according to capacity, prevention of the exploitation of the fruits of labour, and exchange at labour value within and between nations.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: It gives a clear rule for instruments: they embody human mentality, deserve bounded trust, and must have their signals read by people.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: The definiteness of need depends on awakening, which the darshan itself describes as not yet established in human tradition. The economic proposal therefore rests on a prior transformation whose spread has not been demonstrated at scale.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: The valuation of labour by pace, time, and means meets the problem Marx faced in reducing heterogeneous labour to a common measure. Midpoint averages may work for wheat within a village; their extension to complex, multi-stage products made across many places needs the labour-accounting methods discussed in §§4.10 and 8.3, which the treatise does not itself develop.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Coordination beyond the village relies on councils and committees. The information problem that prices address (§4.9) is acknowledged only indirectly, through the transitional use of market rates; §8.4 suggests how records and instruments might supply part of that information.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: The critique of specialisation (AA, pp. 70–71) sits uneasily with the special aspirations the darshan endorses, telephony, broadcasting, and transport, which depend on highly specialised production; the treatise’s own allowance for large industries at higher tiers suggests the objection is to specialisation severed from wholeness, but this is not made explicit.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Several of the treatise’s natural-science claims, on the earth’s magnetic current and on cosmic rays and water, go beyond present evidence and weaken its ecological argument where its general claims are well supported.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan gives the most complete account of why human economies do not reach balance, and its institutional proposal is more specific than most alternatives, but its practicability depends on conditions it has yet to evidence beyond small communities.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.2 Neoclassical economics — coordination without a stopping point

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: It provides powerful tools for coordinating production and exchange among very large numbers of people who do not know one another.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Its methods of measurement, national accounts, input–output analysis, and the study of incentives, are indispensable to any economy that must assess its own condition.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Treating non-satiation as an assumption rather than a doctrine allows its models to be adapted.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: By taking wants as given, it has no account of why they grow and no criterion for when enough has been produced.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Its measure of success, growth of output valued in money, counts depletion of natural assets as income and rewards artificial scarcity.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Its separation of economics from the purposes of human life leaves those purposes to be supplied by whatever wants prevail.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Neoclassical economics coordinates without a stopping point, and its tools can serve a cyclical economy only if that economy supplies the criteria the discipline leaves out.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.3 Marxian and ecological economics — a sound diagnosis on a different ground

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Marx’s analysis of the circuit of capital and of the endlessness of accumulation in money matches the darshan’s critique closely.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Ecological economics grounds the limits of growth in thermodynamics and earth-system science and has developed measures of throughput and planetary boundaries.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Marx’s reliance on class conflict as the motor of change conflicts with the darshan’s account of complementarity and has produced coercive regimes in practice.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Ecological economics explains continued growth by institutions, debt, competition, and employment, without an account of the person whose wants those institutions serve, and so it struggles to make restraint chosen rather than imposed.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Marxian and ecological economics diagnose the open spiral soundly from the side of capital and of nature, and the darshan supplies the side of the person that both leave undeveloped.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.4 Gandhian economics — the closest relative

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Kumarappa’s economy of permanence and Schumacher’s Buddhist economics share the darshan’s village autonomy, cyclical agriculture and energy, production by the many, and restraint of wants.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: They have a long record of practical experiment in Indian villages and in appropriate-technology movements.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Their restraint of wants rests on moral and religious exhortation, simplicity as a virtue, rather than on an account of why wants become insatiable and how understanding makes them definite.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: They give little attention to the valuation of labour and to a staged transition from money exchange.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Gandhian economics is the nearest relative of cyclical economics in practice, and the darshan offers it a foundation in the understanding of jeevan that it lacks.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.5 Advaita and Indian ethics — a diagnosis of desire without an economic architecture

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: The Gita and Advaita give a penetrating account of desire as arising from mistaken identification with body and mind, and agree with the darshan that enjoyment does not quiet desire.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: The ordering of artha under dharma gives wealth a place without making it the aim of life.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Their remedy is directed inward, to knowledge of the Self and detachment, and offers no institutional design for production and exchange.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Treating the empirical world as of lower reality makes the economy a field to be transcended rather than an order to be established.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta and Indian ethics share the darshan’s diagnosis of desire, and the darshan differs in turning the remedy outward into family, production, and exchange.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.6 What the darshan can learn from economics

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Six lessons from economic theory bear directly on cyclical economics. First, coordination beyond the village needs information, and the treatise’s own transitional reliance on market rates shows that prices carry knowledge which councils will have to obtain in some other form; the instruments discussed in §8 are one possible way. Second, prosperity and production security can be evidenced only if they are measured, and national accounting, input–output analysis, material-flow accounting, and life-cycle assessment provide methods for doing so. Third, Ostrom’s work on commons shows that the governance of shared natural assets can be designed and tested, which bears on the village’s jurisdiction over its forests, water, and minerals. Fourth, the theories of human need of Max-Neef, Doyal, and Gough can sharpen the family’s assessment of need and guard it against the charge of paternalism. Fifth, an account of money as it actually works, as credit created through lending, would let the darshan’s critique of symbolic value address present institutions directly rather than a commodity-money system that no longer exists. Sixth, input–output analysis and the long debate over labour-time calculation show how the labour embodied in complex goods can be computed, and what objections such computation must meet (§4.10).

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: 9.7 Open problems

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Several questions remain unsettled.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Need at scale. How does family-level assessment of need aggregate across a district or a nation, and how are disagreements between families’ assessments resolved without either imposing a standard or abandoning definiteness?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Labour valuation for complex goods. How should common values of labour be set and revised when skills, tools, and conditions differ widely, and how far can computed labour values for goods that pass through many hands and places be relied on (§§4.10, 8.3)?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Coordination without prices. What replaces the information carried by prices in the third stage of the transition, and how much can measurement and AI instruments supply (§8.4)?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Automation and participation. How can AI and other machines reduce drudgery and the time production takes without displacing people from production or concentrating control of the means (§8.5)?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Specialisation and the special aspirations. What division of labour is compatible with the darshan’s critique of specialisation, given that telephony, broadcasting, and transport require it?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Transition within a debt economy. How does an exchange-reserve working without interest coexist with banks that create money through interest-bearing loans, and what happens when the guarantor bank’s terms change?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Evidence. What observations in communities practising the darshan would show that needs become definite, that production exceeds need, that producers receive the value of their labour, and that material throughput falls? Systematic observations of this kind remain to be gathered.

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Natural-science claims. Which of the treatise’s claims about the earth’s balance, beyond the general dependence of production on natural regeneration, can be tested, and how should those not supported by present earth science be treated?

passages.heading: 9-critical-review
passages.text: Instruments and judgement. Can communities govern AI systems of the kind described in §8 without ceding to them the judgements of justice, dharma, and truth, and can such systems be kept from being directed towards profit?

passages.heading: 10-conclusion
passages.text: 10. Conclusion

passages.heading: 10-conclusion
passages.text: Human economies do not reach balance because the need they are asked to meet is not the need they can meet. The body’s requirements are definite, and the rest of nature shows what balance with them looks like. Jeevan seeks continuity of happiness, and in delusion it pursues that continuity through the transient satisfactions of selection and taste, reading each failure as a shortage of objects. Accumulation, especially of money, gives this pursuit an object that never decays and never satisfies, and an economy organised around it extracts from the earth without limit and calls its imbalance growth.

passages.heading: 10-conclusion
passages.text: Cyclical economics answers by closing the cycle at the points where it now runs open. Need is assessed and made definite within the family; labour applied to natural abundance produces objects for use; the objects nourish and protect the body and sustain social life, which renews the capacity to produce; labour is valued by the usefulness it establishes, and exchange follows that value, so that remuneration equals production and leaves no room for profit; production stays within the proportions of natural regeneration; and the remainder flows into right use. The economy is one dimension of a self-governing order of families and villages, and it cannot be separated from education, health, and justice.

passages.heading: 10-conclusion
passages.text: Economic theory has much to teach this proposal about coordination, measurement, commons, needs, money, and the calculation of labour values, and modern instruments can make the conditions of the cycle visible far faster than surveys and ledgers alone. The darshan’s distinction between law, regulation, and balance on one side and justice, dharma, and truth on the other gives these instruments a clear place. They can help bring the economy into balance by measuring, accounting, warning, and applying settled rules, and they can help give human labour its true value by recording what labour establishes and what it receives, from the village to the exchange between regions. They must return to people the questions of whether a need is real, an exchange just, a valuation fair, and a use consistent with the order of the whole, and they must be deployed so that every person remains a participant in production. The economy the darshan describes depends finally on understanding, and no instrument can supply that. What instruments can do is show quickly and plainly where understanding is missing.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Cyclical economics (avartansheel arthshastra): the right use, security, and prosperity of resources in the form of body, mind, and wealth, organised as a cycle that returns to its starting point with its purpose fulfilled. The working economy is the cyclical economy (avartansheel arthvyavastha).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Cyclicality (avartansheelta): complementarity and mutual sustenance, a movement that passes through complementary activity towards a goal and returns to its starting point.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Resources (artha): body, mind, and wealth together.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Wealth (dhan): produced objects carrying usefulness value and aesthetic value; not money.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Natural abundance (prakritik aishvarya): earth, air, water, forest, and minerals, the sites where labour is utilised.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Value (mulya): a unit’s participation in the orderliness of the whole; for produced things, their usefulness and aesthetic value.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Value of labour (shram mulya): the value of human labour, judged by the usefulness and aesthetic value it establishes; the basis on which produced objects are valued and exchanged. Valuing labour is the act of evaluating that usefulness and aesthetic value through the labour that established them.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Common aspirations and special aspirations (samanya akanksha, mahatvakanksha): food, shelter, and adornment; telephony, broadcasting, and transport.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Production in excess of need (avashyakta se adhik utpadan): the condition of prosperity in every family.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Prosperity (samriddhi): the absence of the sentiment of lacking; production in excess of need, with its right use and security.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Use, right use, and purposeful use (upyog, sadupyog, prayojansheelta): utilisation of body, mind, and wealth in the nourishment and protection of the body and the motion of society; in orderliness and undivided society; and in evidencing understanding from generation to generation.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Exchange-reserve (vinimay kosh): the village institution through which produced objects are exchanged without profit and loss.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Righteous wealth (svadhan): wealth received as remuneration of one’s own labour, as a gift, or as an award; its opposite is ill-gotten wealth, obtained through exploitation and hypocrisy.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Generosity (udarta): the happy offering of body, mind, and wealth, according to need, for the awakening, health, and prosperity of others.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Accumulation (sangrah): gathering beyond use; hoarding where it exceeds need.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Profit-obsession (labhonmad): the pursuit of giving less and taking more without a satiation point.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Symbolic currency (prateek mudra): metal or paper currency standing for objects; its value is symbolic value.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Satiation point (tripti bindu): the point at which an activity is fulfilled; accumulation, comfort, and profit have none.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Autonomous human (swayatt manav): a person who trusts in oneself, respects excellence, is balanced in talent and personality, social in behaviour, and self-reliant in occupation.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Balance (santulan): the definite, mutually sustaining condition that each order maintains in its existent state; for the human order it is evidenced as resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Law, regulation, and balance (niyam, niyantran, santulan): the orderliness evident in nature, which humans understand and maintain.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Justice, dharma, and truth (nyaya, dharma, satya): the human evaluations of relationship, of participation in universal orderliness, and of coexistence.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Source status of Avartansheel Arthshastra

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Avartansheel Arthshastra (AA) is cited from the project’s working English translation of the 2024 printing, a complete first pass now under the author’s review. AA and the Karm Darshan working translation (KD) are paraphrased with page citations; the block quotations come from Rakesh Gupta’s published translation of Jeevan Vidya. Janvad (JVD) and Adhyatmvad (AVD) are cited from Sanjeev Chopra’s translations in progress. AA, KD, MVD, and JV are cited by printed page, and SB, JVD, and AVD by page in the project’s PDFs. Passages of AA whose Hindi structure is unclear are indexed in the translation workspace; where the argument depends on one, the reading adopted is recorded in the notes below.

passages.heading: editorial-notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The study draws its economic principles from the darshan’s published translations and from the project’s working translations together. The table shows where each principle is stated.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The definition of cyclicality

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The treatise’s definition of cyclicality (AA, p. 15) is flagged as unclear in the translation workspace (U-011). Its central phrase is an unpunctuated compound of natural abundance, naturalness, and natural complementarity, and it is not certain what is “linked”: resources, the process, or the points of the cycle. §3.2 adopts the reading that a cycle starts from any point, passes through complementary activity in the sense of prosperity towards the fulfilment of a goal, and returns to its starting point. This reading is supported by the examples on the same page, by the identification of cyclicality with complementarity and mutual sustenance (AA, p. 42), and by the provision sequence (AA, p. 106). The study’s argument does not depend on choosing among the parsings.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The provision cycle and replenishment

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The project’s introductory primer presents avartansheel as cyclical or replenishing production, attending to what is taken from nature and returned. The Jeevan Vidya lectures define the cycle as the renewal of human capacity through production, nourishment, and social participation (JV, p. 154). The treatise supports both and relates them. The provision cycle is the definition (AA, pp. 26, 106), and the use of natural assets in proportion to their production, without obstructing and while helping their production, is its condition (AA, pp. 114, 142, 146). §3.3 and §3.7 present them in that relation.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Cyclicality and natural recurrence

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The Karm Darshan working translation renders sahajavritti and anukshan-vikshan-vritti as “natural recurrence”. These terms concern the continuity of contemplation in jeevan, not economic or natural cyclicality, and are not used in this study.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The synthesis on insatiability

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: §2.3’s claim that insatiability arises from pursuing a continuous need of jeevan through transient means is assembled from connected passages: the four and a half effective activities and the internal conflict of the rest (JV, pp. 72–73), the inexhaustibility of selection and taste (AA, pp. 17–18), the transience of sensory satisfaction (JV, pp. 162–163; AA, p. 48), the indefiniteness of needs pursued as indulgence (MVD, p. 128), and the regulation of taste by the higher faculties in awakening (AA, p. 95). No single passage states the whole claim, and its phrasing as a “category error” is this study’s.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Pairings of use with justice, resolution, and authenticity

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The treatise pairs usefulness with justice, right use with resolution, and purposeful use with authenticity (AA, p. 116). A later passage describes usefulness as the exposition of the primacy of justice, dharma, and truth “in sequence” (AA, p. 118), which is flagged as unclear (U-129) and may have lost the other two terms of the triad. §3.6 follows the clearer passage.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Specialisation

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The treatise criticises specialisation for losing sight of wholeness, citing pest control and fertiliser that damage the agriculture they were meant to serve (AA, pp. 70–71), and criticises specialists who demand much while producing little (JV, p. 153). It also endorses telephony, broadcasting, and transport as special aspirations and provides for large industries at the higher tiers of self-governance (AA, pp. 29–30, 115). The study reads the criticism as directed at specialisation severed from wholeness and from production, and records the tension in §9.1 and §9.7.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Market rates in the transition

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: In the first stage of exchange, the exchange-reserve values local produce at the nearby wholesale rate less transport (AA, pp. 136–137, 142). This is a transitional use of prices, not a departure from valuation by labour, which the treatise reaches in the third stage. §9.6 reads it also as evidence that prices carry information which a labour-based system will need to obtain in another way.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Artificial intelligence as an application

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The texts do not discuss artificial intelligence. §8 applies the darshan’s distinction between law, regulation, and balance and justice, dharma, and truth (MVD, p. 173; AA, pp. 18, 117), its rule for trusting instruments (KD, p. 139), its criterion for technique (AA, pp. 107, 118; SB, p. 267), and the treatise’s provisions for surveys, committee evaluation, labour valuation, and computer-linked information (AA, pp. 66, 119, 122–125, 132, 138, 145–149), to the question of what an instrument can carry in a cyclical economy. It follows the placement of AI in the material order and the distinction between amplifying and examining uses developed in Artificial Intelligence and Coexistence. The division of tasks proposed there is this study’s extension.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Terminology

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Santulan is rendered as balance throughout, following MVD’s account of each order as balanced in its existent state (MVD, p. 105). “Stability” was considered for the study’s question but would suggest mere persistence, whereas santulan names a mutually sustaining relation with the rest of nature. The English renderings of AA’s economic vocabulary follow the decisions approved for the translation and adopted project-wide in October 2026: cyclical economics and cyclical economy for avartansheel arthshastra and arthvyavastha, cyclicality for avartansheelta, value of labour for shram mulya, production in excess of need for avashyakta se adhik utpadan, satiation point for tripti bindu, exchange-reserve for vinimay kosh, and food, shelter, and adornment for ahar, avas, alankar. Where the published JV translation uses “clothing” for alankar in a quotation, the quotation keeps its wording.
